passage:
I'm Sumit, and last year in Class 4 I was the boy who only shared if I got something back. Chips for chips. Pencil for eraser. I thought that was just fair.
One day Raju's tiffin fell and his rice went all over the floor. I had two parathas. I said, "You can have one if you give me your sticker." He didn't have any stickers.
Urmila Ma'am was on lunch duty. She didn't tell me I was selfish. She crouched down and said, "Sumit, you're good at fair deals. But how would Raju feel if nobody shared with him today?" Then she waited.
I looked at Raju. His eyes were wet. I felt my face get hot. I gave him the paratha. No sticker.
The weird thing is, it felt better than any deal. Now I still like fair, but I also look at people's faces first.

qa.q: What fell on the floor?
qa.a: Raju's tiffin, with his rice.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel when he looked at Raju's wet eyes?
qa.a: His face got hot; he felt a rush of understanding and maybe some embarrassment as he saw how Raju must be feeling.

qa.q: Why was Urmila Ma'am's approach a turning point for Sumit?
qa.a: She praised his fairness instead of calling him selfish and asked how Raju would feel, so Sumit shifted his attention from the trade to Raju's feelings.

qa.q: How might Raju have felt when Sumit gave him the paratha with no sticker?
qa.a: Raju probably felt relieved and cared for, having lost his lunch and then been helped without having to give anything.

grounding: It shows a teacher asking a child how a classmate would feel if nobody shared, turning him from trade toward feelings without shaming his sense of fairness.
